props.title: Shark Attack 3: Megalodon

sections.content: Shark Attack 3: Megalodon (2002) stands as a masterclass in "so bad it's good" filmmaking, joining the pantheon of delightfully terrible shark movies that followed in the wake of Jaws (1975). The film's infamously awful CGI, where the megalodon looks like a Microsoft Paint creation swimming through PlayStation 1-era graphics, makes Deep Blue Sea (1999) look like a documentary. Most notably, it features John Barrowman's improvised pickup line so shocking it became an internet meme, representing the height of early 2000s direct-to-video absurdity.

sections.content: The early 2000s marked a peculiar era for shark films, with digital effects making it cheaper than ever to produce creature features, but budgets rarely matching ambition. Shark Attack 3 (2002) emerged alongside gems like Shark Hunter (2001) and Megalodon (2002), forming an unholy trinity of shark-sploitation that emphasized spectacle over sense. These films paved the way for the self-aware camp of Sharknado (2013) and its numerous sequels.

The film's technical shortcomings - from obvious green screen work to rubber shark props - exemplify the transition period between practical effects and CGI. While Deep Rising (1998) and Lake Placid (1999) managed to blend practical and digital effects effectively, Shark Attack 3 represents the bottom-barrel approach that would later become intentionally comedic in films like Sand Sharks (2011). sections.content: What makes Shark Attack 3 fascinating is its unintentional influence on modern "mockbuster" culture. The Asylum, famous for Mega Shark vs. Giant Octopus (2009) and countless other shark films, learned valuable lessons from this era about marketing outrageous concepts. Today's deliberately campy productions like Ghost Shark (2013) and 6-Headed Shark Attack (2018) owe their existence to the accidental comedy gold of films like Shark Attack 3.
